catalog.name: eel_reproduction_mystery
catalog.description: The enduring biological mystery of how and where Anguilliform eels reproduce. For millennia, the spawning mechanism was unknown; Aristotle speculated eels emerged from mud. The Sargasso Sea spawning ground was discovered only in the 20th century, yet no one has ever observed eels mating in the wild. European and American eels converge from thousands of rivers across two continents into a single ocean basin, metamorphose, spawn at depth, and die — their leptocephalus larvae drifting back on currents. The core mechanism (fertilization, mating behavior, depth, precise conditions) remains unobserved. This is a system where inputs (silver eels departing rivers) and outputs (leptocephali appearing) are known, but the crossing point is obscured.

catalog.description:
The Sargasso Sea: a 2-million-square-mile region of the North Atlantic bounded by four major ocean currents (Gulf Stream, North Atlantic, Canary, North Equatorial) forming a gyre. It is the only sea without a land boundary. Dense with floating sargassum seaweed, it is the known spawning destination of European and American freshwater eels. Yet the precise spawning mechanism — depth, behavior, fertilization, mating ritual — has never been directly observed. The Sea is both a place and a hidden event-horizon: we know eels enter it and leptocephalus larvae exit, but the interior
crossing point remains opaque. The Sea is simultaneously a literal geographical region and a structural occlusion.

catalog.name: anguilliform_eel_life_cycle
catalog.description: The life cycle of Anguilliform freshwater eels: leptocephalus larvae → glass eels → elvers → yellow eels (freshwater growth, 5-20 years) → silver eels (metamorphosis for oceanic migration). A single organism undergoes radical morphological, physiological, and ecological transformations across radically different biomes. The silver eel stage marks the terminal metamorphosis: eyes enlarge, pectoral fins grow, gut atrophies, body silvered for camouflage in open ocean — the eel now carries fat reserves sufficient to cross thousands of miles without feeding. The eel stops eating entirely; its digestive tract dissolves. It is04月swimming toward a death it has never witnessed and a spawning ground encoded somewhere in its body as a navigational imperative. The life cycle forms a closed topological loop — but with the spawning event as the concealed knot.
